Stick Broken Into Three Pieces

ProbabilityCoordinatesParadoxes
Game: Break a stick into three pieces. Can the pieces always be put together into a triangle? Find out where they can and how often they do.
How to play: Drag the point P: its three coloured lines are the pieces. Or pick a way of breaking and break sticks at random.

Look for the math

Three pieces make a triangle only when each is shorter than the other two together, that is, shorter than half the stick (the triangle inequality). How likely that is depends on how you break the stick.

Every break is a point

Make the stick as long as the height of an equilateral triangle. From any point P inside, the three perpendiculars to the sides always add up to the height: that is Viviani's theorem. So each P cuts the stick into three pieces, and each way of cutting it is exactly one P. The three lengths are P's trilinear coordinates. A piece is half the stick on the line joining the midpoints of two sides. So the pieces make a triangle exactly when P is inside the middle triangle, which covers a quarter of the area.

Two random breaks: 1/4

If both break points are uniform on the stick, P is uniform over the big triangle, and the chance is the middle triangle's share of the area: 1/4.

Break the longer piece: 2 ln 2 − 1

Break once, then break the longer piece. A triangle is still needed in one of three equal small triangles, so it is tempting to answer 1/3. Martin Gardner printed that, and corrected it later. P is no longer spread evenly. If the short piece has length h, the second break succeeds with chance h/(1−h). Averaging over h from 0 to 1/2 gives

2 ∫01/2 h/(1−h) dh = 2 ln 2 − 1 ≈ 0.386

If a coin decides which piece to break, half the time it is the short one and no triangle can come out, so the chance is ln 2 − 1/2 ≈ 0.193. If a piece is picked with chance equal to its length, the answer is 1/4 again: that is just another way of choosing two uniform points. The logic test integrated all four over a fine grid and broke 100,000 random sticks each way; the results matched.

Choose “once, then the longer piece” and press Break 1000 a few times. Does the count settle near 1/3 or near 0.386?
